The plan already has a number baked in: [plan/04-stage2-model.md:14](plan/04-stage2-model.md:14) sets **~300 real strikes across 2-3 fights** as the floor "before this is worth training" — that's not a number I'm inventing, it's the threshold Stage 0 was scoped against.

But treat that as a floor to get a first signal, not a number that guarantees the model "works as expected." Two things to watch:

- **Class imbalance dominates at this scale.** 300 strikes split across strike family × target (jab/cross/hook × head/body, kicks, clinch knees, etc.) means some classes could land in single digits after a held-out eval split. The model will be fine on common strikes and useless on rare ones no matter how much you pad the total count — which is exactly the case for controlling event-type mix per-event, from the review feature we just discussed, rather than just labelling more of whatever's easiest to find.
- **This is a start-and-iterate loop, not a one-shot target.** Train on ~300, run error analysis on where it's wrong (likely landed-vs-missed, given depth is invisible to 2D pose per [plan/04-stage2-model.md:36](plan/04-stage2-model.md:36)), then label more data specifically for the failure modes rather than guessing a bigger upfront number. Active-learning-style growth beats trying to hit some large N before ever training.

So: hit ~300 to get moving, but budget for at least one more labelling pass once you see where it actually fails.
I am not asking about the plan markdowns. I want you real world feedback on amount of input events

Fair — stripping away what the repo doc claims, here's the honest calculus for this specific setup (pose-keypoint window classifier over strike family × target, small ST-GCN/temporal-CNN, per [plan/04-stage2-model.md](plan/04-stage2-model.md)):

**Per-class, not total, is what matters.** "300 events" only means something once you divide by class count. If you're classifying ~10-15 combinations (jab/cross/hook/kick × head/body/leg, clinch knees, etc.), 300 total events averages to 20-30 per class before imbalance, and the common classes will eat most of that. For a small deep model to generalize on skeleton sequences — even a narrow, constrained one like this — you want closer to **150-300 examples of the class itself**, not 150-300 total. So realistically you're looking at low thousands of total labeled strikes before every class the model needs to distinguish is individually well-represented, not hundreds.

**Diversity across fights matters more than raw count.** 300 strikes from 2-3 fights means 2-3 camera setups, 4-6 fighters' body proportions, one or two gyms'/promotions' framing conventions. A model trained on that will likely overfit to those specific fighters and camera angles rather than learning the strike itself — it'll look great on held-out clips from the *same* fights and fall apart on a new fight. Spreading the same total count across more fights (even at fewer strikes each) generalizes better than concentrating it.

**Start smaller than "production," on purpose.** Given that, I'd treat ~300 not as "enough to train the real model" but as enough to prove the pipeline works end-to-end (export → windowing → training loop → eval) and to see which classes are catastrophically underrepresented. Then use that failure signal to decide what to label next — which is a good argument for the per-event review feature giving you class-level control, since you'll want to deliberately backfill rare classes rather than labeling fights front-to-back.

**Bottom line:** for something you'd trust in predictions, plan on needing an order of magnitude more than 300 — realistically 1,500-3,000+ labeled strikes across as many distinct fights as you can get, not 2-3 — with 300 being a useful early checkpoint, not the target.
Can there be too much training data?

Not in the sense of literally too many examples hurting the model directly — more data almost never makes a model worse by itself. The real risks are indirect:

- **Bad labels compound.** If there's a systematic labeling error (e.g. the corner-swap ambiguity or circular round labels you've hit before), more volume just means more confidently-wrong examples reinforcing the same bias, not more signal. Quality ceiling matters more than quantity once you're past the point of just checking the pipeline works.
- **Class imbalance gets worse, not better, by scaling everything up uniformly.** If jabs outnumber spinning back kicks 50:1 at 300 events, they'll still outnumber them 50:1 at 30,000 — the model just gets more confident about ignoring the rare class rather than better at it. Volume without deliberate rebalancing entrenches skew.
- **Diminishing returns hit early for narrow tasks.** This isn't an open-ended vision problem; it's a small, constrained classification task. Past some point (probably low-to-mid thousands here, not millions), each additional labeled strike buys very little — the cost (labeling time, review time) stops being worth it and that effort is better spent on diversity (more fights/camera angles) or targeted rare-class collection than raw count.
- **Overfitting to your own data's blind spots.** If all your fights share a camera angle, ruleset, or promotion, a huge pile of that data teaches the model your setup, not fighting in general — it'll look great on your eval split and fail on anything novel.

So the practical answer: no upper bound where more data actively degrades things, but there's a point — probably well before you'd expect — where more data stops helping and effort is better spent on label quality and class/fight diversity instead of volume.

Concretely, given what's actually in the pipeline right now: there's no real cut detector (only an OCR-timer-based replay detector in [fight_segmentation.py](ai/video_processing/fight_segmentation.py) that's unrelated to true camera cuts), and the tracker has no cut-awareness at all — a hard cut can silently re-match a geometry-based slot to the wrong person, carrying the wrong skeleton along with it ([FighterTracker.py](ai/models/FighterTracker.py), flagged as an open weak point in [box_smoothing.py:77-84](ai/video_processing/box_smoothing.py:77)). That matters directly for this question, since [your own memory](tracker-swaps-at-cuts-and-clinches.md) already flags cuts as exactly where corner swaps cluster.

Practical handling:

1. **Still label the strike — don't drop it.** It happened; the event itself is real signal for scoring/counting even if the surrounding video is messy.
2. **Flag the span as unreliable using the `excluded` mechanism that already exists** ([Annotate.tsx](frontend/src/pages/Annotate.tsx:226), `P` key), rather than building a real cut detector right now. At ~300 events you're already scrubbing frame-by-frame by hand — a human catches a cut trivially, and a histogram-based auto-detector was already ruled unreliable for MMA cuts. Automate this later once volume justifies the engineering cost, not now.
3. **Distrust `fighter_id` specifically, not just the strike class, near a cut.** Since corner swaps concentrate at cuts, a punch labeled right after one deserves extra scrutiny on *which fighter* threw it — this is a good concrete case for the confirm/decline review feature from earlier: flag "near a cut" events for mandatory re-check rather than treating all events as equally trustworthy.
4. **For training specifically, once `export.py` exists:** a ~1s window that straddles a cut is a discontinuous keypoint trajectory glued together from two different framings — that's actively harmful training data, not just noisy. The window should be skipped entirely if it overlaps an `excluded`/cut span, not truncated or kept — with data this scarce, better to lose one example than poison the model with a physically incoherent motion sequence.

What should be the lenght of the clips/frames fed into training data?

For a pose-keypoint strike classifier, I'd go with **about 1 second, placed off-centre: roughly 0.6 s before the labelled frame and 0.3–0.4 s after it**. Use the same length for every strike type.

**Why that length**

- **How long strikes take.** A jab takes about 150–250 ms from start to full extension. Hooks and crosses take 250–400 ms. Kicks take 400–700 ms, plus the time to load them. One second covers the whole motion of even the slower strikes.
- **The part before impact tells you the most.** Weight shift, hip turn and the shoulder dropping are what separate a jab from a cross, or a hook from an overhand. That's why more of the window sits before the labelled frame.
- **A short tail after impact helps with landed vs missed.** Recoil, the head snapping back or the arm over-extending on a miss all show up there. Past about 0.4 s you're just seeing the reset.

**Why not shorter or longer**

- **Under ~0.5 s:** you cut off the wind-up. Jab vs cross and hook vs overhand get much harder to tell apart.
- **Over ~1.5 s:**
  - **Combinations:** strikes in a combo land 200–300 ms apart, so each window holds several strikes and the label gets ambiguous.
  - **Camera cuts:** broadcast MMA cuts often. Every window that crosses a cut gets thrown out, so longer windows cost you a lot of examples when you have little data.
  - **Clinch and ground:** more of the window becomes clinch or ground movement with nothing to do with the strike.

**Details that matter as much as the length**

- **Set the window in seconds and resample every clip to one frame rate.** Your videos won't all have the same fps. Your tracker constants suggest you process at about 50 fps (0.6 s = 30 frames). Stay at 30 fps or higher: at 25 fps a jab is only 4–5 frames.
- **Shift the window randomly by a few frames (±3–5) during training.** A human-marked impact frame is only accurate to a few frames. Without the shift, the model learns your labelling habits instead of the strike.
- **Train on "no strike" windows too, and plenty of them.** At prediction time almost every window contains no strike. Include about 3–5 no-strike windows for every strike. Take them at least half a window away from any labelled strike. Favour hard cases: feints, pawing jabs, clinch pummelling, level changes.
- **Fight state needs a longer window than strikes.** Telling standing from clinch from ground takes 2–3 seconds of context. With a shared 1 s window, either the state output gets noisy or the strike output gets muddied. Give state its own longer window, or smooth its per-frame predictions over time.

To start, use 1.0 s at 30 fps with the window running from −0.6 s to +0.4 s. Once you have enough data to compare, try 0.8 s and 1.2 s and keep whichever scores better on held-out fights.
